name: The Caledonian Hotel
description: Built between 1899 and 1903 by the Caledonian Railway Company as the grand terminus hotel for its Princes Street Station, the hotel's red sandstone facade was quarried at Locharbriggs and Corncockle in Dumfriesshire and brought to Edinburgh on the company's own trains. Inside, marble columns, gilded ceilings and 205 guest rooms greeted arriving passengers, who could once step straight from the platforms through three archways into the hotel itself. Long known simply as "The Caley", it outlived the station by decades: passenger trains stopped running from Princes Street in September 1965 and the tracks were lifted, but the hotel above kept operating, still the grandest address at the west end of Princes Street.
interesting_fact: The Caledonian's engineers once piped waste steam from locomotives at the adjoining station straight into the hotel's boilers to help heat its water - a literal recycling of the railway's own exhaust. Its corridors are noticeably wide, reputedly built generously enough for two Edwardian ladies in full hooped skirts to pass without their dresses touching. Over the twentieth century its guest book filled with the famous - Charlie Chaplin, Laurel and Hardy, Elizabeth Taylor, Bing Crosby, Gene Kelly, who is said to have danced down the main staircase, and Sean Connery, a regular guest over the decades until his death in 2020. More recently Taylor Swift stayed here during her 2024 Eras Tour dates in Edinburgh.

name: Dean Ramsay Memorial
address: St John's Episcopal Church, Princes Street, Edinburgh EH1 2EP
description: This soaring Celtic cross, over 8 metres of Shap granite on three broad steps, stands in the graveyard of St John's Episcopal Church at the west end of Princes Street, commemorating Edward Bannerman Ramsay, the church's minister for over 40 years and Dean of Edinburgh from 1841 until his death in 1872. Designed by the architect Robert Rowand Anderson and erected in 1879, the cross carries a set of bronze relief panels cast by F. A. Skidmore of Coventry, depicting scenes from Christ's Passion, the Resurrection and Ascension alongside six acts of charity - fitting for a man remembered as much for his philanthropy as for his ministry.
interesting_fact: Dean Ramsay's lasting fame rests less on his sermons than on a single book: "Reminiscences of Scottish Life and Character", a collection of anecdotes and observations on the Scottish national character first published in 1858. It became one of the runaway publishing successes of Victorian Scotland, running through 22 editions by the time of his death in 1872 alone, and it stayed in print well into the 20th century. Ramsay was also a co-founder of Glenalmond College, one of Scotland's leading independent schools, and served as minister of St John's - the church whose churchyard this cross now stands in - from 1830 right through to his death.

name: Mather's Bar
description: This single-room corner bar occupies the ground floor of a five-storey building put up in 1900 by the architects Sydney Mitchell & Wilson for the National Commercial Bank of Scotland. Wine merchant Hugh Mather took over the ground floor in 1902 and established the licensed premises the following year, giving the pub its name, which still runs in gold lettering across the frontage: "Wines. H.P. Mather. Spirits." Inside, the pub has changed remarkably little in well over a century - high ceilings with ornate plasterwork, a large stained-glass window, floor-to-ceiling tiling in the porch, and an original bar counter and half-height panelling.
interesting_fact: CAMRA (the Campaign for Real Ale) has identified Mather's as having a nationally important historic pub interior, one of a small number in Scotland to earn that distinction - meaning the fixtures and layout are protected as being of outstanding historic value, not just an old-looking pub but a genuinely preserved one. Tucked just off the west end of Princes Street, it's long been a classic "old man's bar" popular with people passing through on their way to the trams, buses, or the theatre nearby, rather than a tourist destination in its own right.

name: Statue of Sir James Young Simpson
description: This seated bronze figure in academic robes, book resting on one knee, was erected by public subscription in 1877 and designed by the sculptor William Brodie. It commemorates Sir James Young Simpson, professor of midwifery at Edinburgh University, who in November 1847 became the first doctor to demonstrate chloroform's use as an anaesthetic - testing it first on himself and two colleagues at his own dinner table before adopting it in his obstetric practice. The discovery transformed surgery and childbirth almost overnight, sparing patients an era of fully conscious operations.
interesting_fact: Chloroform anaesthesia faced fierce religious objection at first - some clergy argued that easing the pain of childbirth defied the biblical curse on Eve - until Queen Victoria herself was given chloroform by her physician during the birth of Prince Leopold in 1853, an endorsement that effectively ended the controversy overnight. Simpson became one of the most celebrated Scots of his era: knighted in 1866, the first doctor in Scotland to receive the honour, and when he died in 1870 more than 100,000 people are said to have lined Edinburgh's streets for his funeral procession to Warriston Cemetery.
